subject: biology
overview: This unit covers the cell as the structural and functional unit of life: cell theory, prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisation, cell organelles, the chemistry of life (biomolecules and enzymes), and how cells divide (cell cycle, mitosis, meiosis). It is one of the highest-weightage units in NEET Biology. Most questions are direct, NCERT-line based, and often framed as match-the-list, statement pairs or multi-statement items.

topics.explanation: Anton von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell. Robert Brown later discovered the nucleus. In 1838 Matthias Schleiden, a German botanist, observed that all plants are made of different kinds of cells that form tissues. In 1839 Theodore Schwann, a British zoologist, studied animal cells. He reported that cells have a thin outer layer, now called the plasma membrane, and that the cell wall is unique to plant cells. Together, Schleiden and Schwann proposed the cell theory. It did not explain how new cells form. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow added that new cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula). Modern cell theory states two things. First, all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells. Second, all cells arise from pre-existing cells. An organism made of one cell is unicellular, and one made of many cells is multicellular. Anything less than a complete cell cannot live independently.
key_points: Leeuwenhoek: first to see a live cell
Robert Brown: discovered the nucleus
Schleiden (1838, plants) and Schwann (1839, animals) formulated cell theory
Schwann: plasma membrane in animal cells; cell wall unique to plants
Virchow (1855): Omnis cellula-e cellula, which completed the theory
Cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of life
topics.neet_tip: Direct name-and-contribution questions (who formulated it, who added 'cells arise from pre-existing cells') are very common.
topics.topic: Cell theory and cell as the basic unit of life

topics.explanation: Prokaryotic cells include bacteria, blue-green algae (cyanobacteria), mycoplasma and PPLO. They lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Their genetic material is naked and circular and lies in the nucleoid. Many also carry plasmids, which are small circular extrachromosomal DNA and may confer antibiotic resistance. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, made of 50S and 30S subunits. Mesosomes, inclusion bodies and gas vacuoles may also be present. Eukaryotic cells occur in protists, fungi, plants and animals. They have a true nucleus with a nuclear envelope, membrane-bound organelles, 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes and a cytoskeleton. Plant cells differ from animal cells in having a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole. Animal cells have centrioles, which are absent in almost all plant cells. Cell size varies widely. Mycoplasma is the smallest cell (about $0.3\ \mu m$), bacteria are 3 to $5\ \mu m$, a human RBC is about $7\ \mu m$, and the ostrich egg is the largest isolated single cell.
key_points: Prokaryotes: bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma, PPLO; fungi are eukaryotes
Bacterial shapes: bacillus (rod), coccus (spherical), vibrio (comma), spirillum (spiral)
Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles, so no peroxisomes, mitochondria or ER
70S ribosomes (50S + 30S) in prokaryotes; 80S (60S + 40S) in eukaryotes
Polysome (polyribosome): several ribosomes on one mRNA
Plant cell: cell wall, plastids, large vacuole; animal cell: centrioles
Smallest cell: Mycoplasma; longest cells: nerve cells; largest isolated cell: ostrich egg

formulas.meaning: Svedberg units measure sedimentation rate, which depends on size and shape, so subunit S values are not additive. This applies equally to $80S$ = $60S$ + $40S$.

topics.neet_tip: Expect multi-statement items on prokaryotic features (plasmid, mesosome, 70S ribosome) mixed with a eukaryote-only feature such as peroxisomes.
topics.topic: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells; plant and animal cells

topics.explanation: The bacterial cell envelope has three tightly bound layers: an outer glycocalyx, the cell wall and the plasma membrane. The glycocalyx may be a loose slime layer or a thick, tough capsule. Gram staining divides bacteria into Gram-positive (retain the stain) and Gram-negative (do not). The mesosome is formed by extension of the plasma membrane into the cell. It helps in cell wall formation, DNA replication and its distribution to daughter cells, respiration, secretion, and increasing membrane surface area and enzyme content. Flagella move bacteria; pili and fimbriae do not help in motility but help attachment. The eukaryotic plasma membrane mainly contains lipids (phospholipids in a bilayer) and proteins. The human RBC membrane has about 52% protein and 40% lipid. Singer and Nicolson's fluid mosaic model (1972) describes a quasi-fluid lipid bilayer that allows lateral movement of proteins. Plant cell walls contain cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins, while algal walls contain cellulose, galactans, mannans and calcium carbonate. The middle lamella is mainly calcium pectate.
key_points: Cell envelope = glycocalyx + cell wall + plasma membrane
Bacterial flagellum: filament, hook and basal body
Pili and fimbriae: attachment, not motility
Fluid mosaic model: Singer and Nicolson (1972)
Membrane proteins: peripheral (surface) and integral (buried)
Membrane fluidity aids growth, intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division
Transport: passive (along gradient, including osmosis), active (uses ATP, e.g. $Na^+/K^+$ pump)
Primary wall can grow; secondary wall forms on the inner side of the primary wall
Plasmodesmata connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring plant cells
topics.neet_tip: Questions ask for the fluid mosaic model's proposers, the RBC membrane protein:lipid ratio, middle lamella composition and mesosome functions.
topics.topic: Cell envelope, cell membrane and cell wall

topics.explanation: The endomembrane system consists of the ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles, because their functions are coordinated. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not included. The ER divides the cytoplasm into luminal and extraluminal compartments. Rough ER carries ribosomes, is involved in protein synthesis and secretion, and is extensive in secretory cells. Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is the major site of lipid synthesis; in animals it synthesises steroidal hormones. The Golgi apparatus was first observed by Camillo Golgi in 1898. It consists of flat, disc-shaped cisternae with a convex cis (forming) face and a concave trans (maturing) face. It packages materials for intracellular targets or for secretion, and it is the site where glycoproteins and glycolipids are formed. Lysosomes bud off from the Golgi and contain acid hydrolases (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) that work best at acidic pH. Vacuoles are bounded by the tonoplast and can occupy up to 90% of a plant cell's volume.
key_points: Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles
RER: protein synthesis; SER: lipid and steroid synthesis
Golgi: cis face receives material from the ER; trans face releases it
Golgi forms glycoproteins and glycolipids and packages secretions
Lysosomes: acid hydrolases, optimally active at acidic pH
Tonoplast transports ions into the vacuole against the gradient, so sap concentration exceeds cytoplasm
Contractile vacuole in Amoeba: osmoregulation and excretion
Food vacuoles in protists are formed by engulfing food particles
topics.neet_tip: NEET checks endomembrane membership (excluding mitochondria, plastids and peroxisomes) and SER versus RER functions.
topics.topic: Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi bodies, lysosomes and vacuoles

topics.explanation: Mitochondria are sausage-shaped or cylindrical organelles. They are about 0.2 to 1.0 $\mu m$ wide (average 0.5) and 1.0 to 4.1 $\mu m$ long. They have a double membrane. The inner membrane encloses the matrix and folds into cristae, which increase surface area. Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration and ATP production, the 'powerhouse of the cell'. The matrix contains circular DNA, a few RNA molecules, 70S ribosomes and components for protein synthesis, and mitochondria divide by fission. Plastids are of three types. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carotenoids and carry out photosynthesis. Chromoplasts contain fat-soluble carotenoids such as carotene and xanthophylls, giving yellow, orange or red colours. Leucoplasts are colourless storage plastids: amyloplasts store starch, elaioplasts store oils and fats, and aleuroplasts store proteins. In a chloroplast, thylakoids are flattened sacs in the stroma, stacked as grana and joined by stroma lamellae. The stroma also contains enzymes, circular DNA and 70S ribosomes. Ribosomes are non-membranous RNA-protein particles first observed by George Palade (1953). Microbodies are single-membrane vesicles with enzymes and include peroxisomes and glyoxysomes.
key_points: Inner mitochondrial membrane encloses the matrix; cristae are its infoldings
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are semi-autonomous: own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes
Chromoplast: carotene and xanthophyll pigments
Amyloplast: starch (e.g. potato); elaioplast: oils; aleuroplast: proteins
Chloroplast: about 5 to 10 $\mu m$ long, 2 to 4 $\mu m$ wide
Chlamydomonas has a single chloroplast; leaf mesophyll cells have 20 to 40
Chloroplast ribosomes are smaller (70S) than cytoplasmic ribosomes (80S)
Ribosomes: no membrane; discovered by Palade
Microbodies occur in both plant and animal cells
topics.neet_tip: Match-list items pair cristae, cisternae, thylakoids and stroma with their locations; plastid–stored substance pairs are frequent.

topics.explanation: The cytoskeleton is a network of proteinaceous filaments in the cytoplasm. It has three components: microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments. It provides mechanical support, motility and maintenance of cell shape. Cilia are small and work like oars, while flagella are longer and responsible for cell movement. Both are hair-like outgrowths of the plasma membrane. Their core, the axoneme, has nine pairs of doublet peripheral microtubules and a pair of central microtubules (9+2 arrangement). The central tubules are joined by bridges and enclosed by a central sheath. Each peripheral doublet is connected to the central sheath by a radial spoke, and adjacent doublets are joined by linkers. Cilia and flagella arise from centriole-like basal bodies. The centrosome contains two cylindrical centrioles lying perpendicular to each other, surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar material. Each centriole has a cartwheel organisation of nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin, each a triplet, with a central proteinaceous hub. Centrioles form the basal body of cilia and flagella and the spindle fibres of animal cells.
key_points: Cytoskeleton: microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments
Axoneme of cilia and flagella: 9+2 microtubule arrangement
Peripheral fibrils of axoneme are doublets; of centriole are triplets
Centriole: 9+0 cartwheel with central hub and radial spokes
Two centrioles in the centrosome lie perpendicular to each other
Prokaryotic flagella differ structurally from eukaryotic flagella
Centrioles absent in almost all higher plant cells
topics.neet_tip: Questions contrast doublets in the axoneme with triplets in the centriole, the 9+2 versus 9+0 pattern, and centriole roles.

topics.explanation: The nucleus was first described by Robert Brown in 1831, and Flemming named the stainable material chromatin. The interphase nucleus has loose nucleoprotein fibres (chromatin), a nuclear matrix and one or more nucleoli. The nuclear envelope has two parallel membranes separated by a 10 to 50 nm perinuclear space. The outer membrane is usually continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes. Nuclear pores allow RNA and protein to move in both directions. Normally there is one nucleus per cell. Mature mammalian RBCs and plant sieve tube cells lack a nucleus. Nucleoli are non-membrane-bound, spherical sites of active ribosomal RNA synthesis and are larger and more numerous in cells active in protein synthesis. Chromatin contains DNA, basic histone proteins, non-histone proteins and RNA. A single human cell has about 2 m of DNA in 46 chromosomes. Each chromosome has a primary constriction (centromere) bearing disc-shaped kinetochores. By centromere position, chromosomes are metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric and telocentric. Some have a satellite beyond a secondary constriction.
key_points: Nucleus discovered by Robert Brown (1831); chromatin named by Flemming
Perinuclear space: 10 to 50 nm
Outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the ER
Nucleolus: rRNA synthesis, no membrane
Enucleate cells: mammalian RBCs, sieve tube cells
Metacentric: middle centromere, equal arms
Sub-metacentric: centromere slightly away from the middle
Acrocentric: centromere near the end; telocentric: terminal centromere
Kinetochores: disc-shaped structures on the sides of the centromere
topics.neet_tip: Common items cover chromosome types by centromere position, nucleolus function, perinuclear space width and enucleate cells.
topics.topic: Nucleus: nuclear membrane, chromatin and nucleolus

topics.explanation: Living tissue contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in higher proportion than the earth's crust. In the human body by weight, oxygen is about 65%, carbon 18.5%, hydrogen 9.5% and nitrogen 3.3%. Water is the most abundant compound in cells. Chemical analysis separates an acid-soluble pool of micromolecules (molecular weight below 1000 Da) from an acid-insoluble fraction. The acid-insoluble fraction contains proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids. Lipids are not polymers but appear here because membranes break into insoluble vesicles. Proteins are heteropolymers of 20 amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Their structure has primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary levels. Polysaccharides are chains of monosaccharides joined by glycosidic bonds. Cellulose is a homopolymer of glucose; starch stores energy and gives a blue colour with iodine; inulin is a fructose polymer; chitin forms exoskeletons. Lipids include fatty acids, glycerides and phospholipids such as lecithin. Nucleic acids are polynucleotides linked by phosphodiester bonds. Watson–Crick B-DNA has 10 bp per turn and a pitch of 3.4 nm.
key_points: Human body by weight: O (65%) > C (18.5%) > H (9.5%) > N (3.3%)
Water: about 70 to 90% of cell mass
RuBisCO: most abundant protein in the biosphere; collagen: most abundant in the animal world
Protein functions: antibody (fights infection), GLUT-4 (glucose transport), receptors, hormones, enzymes
Concanavalin A is a lectin, a secondary metabolite
Amino acids exist as zwitterions; their structure changes with pH
Starch helix holds $I_2$ (blue colour); cellulose does not
Palmitic acid: 16 C including carboxyl C; arachidonic acid: 20 C
Nucleoside = base + sugar; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate
Haemoglobin: 4 subunits ($2\alpha$ + $2\beta$), quaternary structure

formulas.meaning: Chargaff's rule for double-stranded DNA; use it to find unknown base percentages.
Length of B-DNA from the number of base pairs; one turn (10 bp) = 3.4 nm.

topics.neet_tip: Match lists pair biomolecules with functions (starch, antibody, lectin, GLUT-4); elemental-abundance order and bond types are frequent.
topics.topic: Biomolecules: proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids

topics.explanation: Almost all enzymes are proteins; some nucleic acids, called ribozymes, also act as catalysts. Enzymes lower activation energy and speed up reactions. For example, carbonic anhydrase increases the rate of $CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3$ about 10 million times. Substrate binds the active site to form an enzyme–substrate complex, which is transient. The substrate then changes to a transition state and finally to products. Enzyme activity depends on temperature, pH and substrate concentration. Each enzyme shows an optimum temperature and an optimum pH. High temperature denatures enzymes, whereas low temperature only inactivates them temporarily. A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site; for example, malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase. Enzymes are named with the suffix '-ase' and grouped into six classes. Many enzymes need cofactors: prosthetic groups (haem in peroxidase and catalase), coenzymes (NAD and NADP, which contain niacin) and metal ions (zinc in carboxypeptidase). The protein part alone is the apoenzyme.
key_points: Six classes in order: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases
Hydrolases break bonds using water; ligases join two compounds
Lyases remove groups other than by hydrolysis, forming double bonds
Holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor
Prosthetic group is tightly bound; coenzyme binds only transiently
Activity at $V_{max}$ does not rise further with more substrate, because active sites are saturated
Competitive inhibitors are used to control bacterial pathogens
Enzymes from thermophilic organisms in hot springs are stable at 80 to 90 degrees C

formulas.meaning: Michaelis–Menten relation; $K_m$ is the substrate concentration at which $V = \frac{V_{max}}{2}$, and a lower $K_m$ means higher affinity.

topics.neet_tip: Expect EC class identification, cofactor examples (haem, NAD, zinc), the malonate–succinic dehydrogenase pair and effects of temperature and pH.
topics.topic: Enzymes: types, properties, action, classification and nomenclature

topics.explanation: The cell cycle is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and divides into two daughter cells. A typical human cell in culture divides about once every 24 hours, and yeast takes about 90 minutes. The cycle has an interphase, which takes more than 95% of the time, and an M phase lasting about an hour. In G1 the cell is metabolically active and grows, but its DNA does not replicate. In S phase DNA replication occurs, so the DNA content doubles from 2C to 4C while the chromosome number stays the same. In animal cells the centriole also duplicates in the cytoplasm during S phase. G2 continues protein synthesis in preparation for mitosis, and cell growth continues. Cells that stop dividing, such as many heart cells, exit G1 into the quiescent G0 stage. G0 cells stay metabolically active and can be triggered to divide. In animals mitosis occurs only in diploid somatic cells, whereas in plants both haploid and diploid cells can divide mitotically.
key_points: Correct sequence: G1 → S → G2 → M
Interphase (resting phase) = G1 + S + G2, more than 95% of the cycle
Human cell cycle about 24 h; M phase about 1 h; yeast about 90 min
S phase: DNA 2C → 4C, ploidy unchanged
Centriole duplication in animal cells: S phase
G0: quiescent, metabolically active, not proliferating
Meristematic tissues divide continuously throughout life

formulas.meaning: DNA content doubles in S phase while chromosome number (2n) remains constant.

topics.neet_tip: Phase-sequence questions and DNA-content versus chromosome-number questions at G1, G2 and after division are very common.

topics.explanation: Mitosis is called equational division because daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent. Karyokinesis has four stages. Prophase: chromatin condenses, the centrosome moves to opposite poles and spindle fibres form. By its end, the Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus and nuclear envelope are no longer visible. Metaphase: chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, align at the metaphase plate. Spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores. This stage is best for studying chromosome morphology. Anaphase: centromeres split, and the separated chromatids, now daughter chromosomes, move to opposite poles. Telophase: chromosomes decondense at the poles, and the nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi and ER reform. Cytokinesis follows. In animal cells a furrow in the plasma membrane deepens and divides the cytoplasm. In plant cells a cell plate forms in the centre and grows outward; it becomes the middle lamella. If karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, a multinucleate syncytium forms, such as the liquid endosperm of coconut. Mitosis enables growth, repair, cell replacement and maintenance of the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio.
key_points: Stages in order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
Metaphase: best stage to study chromosome morphology
Anaphase: centromeres split and chromatids separate
Animal cytokinesis: furrow; plant cytokinesis: cell plate (middle lamella)
Syncytium example: liquid endosperm of coconut
Mitosis keeps ploidy constant (2n → 2n, or n → n in plants)
Mitosis restores the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio

formulas.meaning: Number of cells formed from one cell after n successive mitotic divisions.

topics.neet_tip: NEET asks stage-specific events (kinetochore attachment, centromere splitting, nuclear envelope reappearance) and the plant versus animal cytokinesis difference.

topics.explanation: Meiosis is a reductional division that produces four haploid cells from one diploid cell. It occurs during gamete formation in sexually reproducing organisms. It involves a single round of DNA replication followed by two divisions. Prophase I is long and has five sub-stages. In leptotene, chromosomes become visible. In zygotene, homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) through the synaptonemal complex, forming bivalents (tetrads). In pachytene, crossing over occurs at recombination nodules with the help of the enzyme recombinase. In diplotene, the synaptonemal complex dissolves and chiasmata appear; in oocytes this stage can last months or years. In diakinesis, chiasmata terminalise, chromosomes are fully condensed, the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down. In anaphase I, homologues separate while sister chromatids stay together. Interkinesis is short and has no DNA replication. Meiosis II resembles normal mitosis, and its anaphase II separates sister chromatids. Meiosis conserves chromosome number across generations and generates genetic variation.
key_points: Prophase I order: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis
Zygotene: synapsis, synaptonemal complex, bivalent
Pachytene: crossing over, recombination nodules, recombinase
Diplotene: chiasmata visible; long-lasting in oocytes
Diakinesis: terminalisation; chromosomes fully condensed for metaphase I
Anaphase I separates homologues; anaphase II separates sister chromatids
Meiosis II, not meiosis I, resembles mitosis
Significance: halves chromosome number in gametes; restores it on fertilisation; creates variation

formulas.meaning: One meiosis yields four haploid cells; useful in counting meioses needed for a given number of gametes or seeds.

topics.neet_tip: Statement-pair and sequence questions focus on prophase I sub-stages (synapsis, crossing over, chiasmata, terminalisation) and which division resembles mitosis.

key_facts: Cell theory: Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839); modified by Virchow (1855).
Smallest cell: Mycoplasma (about $0.3\ \mu m$); human RBC about $7\ \mu m$; bacteria 3 to $5\ \mu m$.
Fluid mosaic model: Singer and Nicolson, 1972.
Human RBC membrane: about 52% protein and 40% lipid.
Prokaryotic ribosome 70S (50S + 30S); eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosome 80S (60S + 40S).
Golgi apparatus was first observed by Camillo Golgi in 1898.
Ribosomes were first observed by George Palade in 1953.
Nucleus was discovered by Robert Brown in 1831.
Vacuole can occupy up to 90% of plant cell volume.
Middle lamella is mainly calcium pectate.
Mitochondria: 0.2 to 1.0 $\mu m$ diameter, 1.0 to 4.1 $\mu m$ length.
Chloroplasts per mesophyll cell: 20 to 40; Chlamydomonas has one.
Perinuclear space: 10 to 50 nm.
A human diploid cell contains about 2 m of DNA in 46 chromosomes.
Axoneme is 9+2 (doublets); centriole is 9+0 (triplets).
Human body by weight: O 65%, C 18.5%, H 9.5%, N 3.3%.
Most abundant protein in the biosphere: RuBisCO; in animals: collagen.
B-DNA: 10 bp per turn, pitch 3.4 nm, 0.34 nm between adjacent base pairs.
Carbonic anhydrase speeds $CO_2$ hydration about 10 million times.
Malonate competitively inhibits succinic dehydrogenase.
Enzyme classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases.
Zinc is a cofactor of carboxypeptidase; haem is the prosthetic group of peroxidase and catalase.
Human cell cycle about 24 h; yeast about 90 min; M phase about 1 h.
Crossing over occurs in pachytene and is mediated by recombinase.
Liquid endosperm of coconut is a syncytium (karyokinesis without cytokinesis).
Chromoplasts contain carotene and xanthophylls; aleuroplasts store proteins; elaioplasts store oils.
common_traps: Including mitochondria, chloroplasts or peroxisomes in the endomembrane system is wrong: it comprises only the ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles.
Assuming S phase doubles chromosome number is wrong: DNA doubles (2C to 4C), but chromosome number stays 2n.
Thinking meiosis I resembles mitosis is wrong: meiosis II resembles mitosis, while meiosis I is reductional.
Adding Svedberg units ($50S + 30S = 80S$) is wrong: the result is 70S, because S values are not additive.
Calling fungi prokaryotes is wrong: fungi are eukaryotes. Prokaryotes are bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma and PPLO.
Assuming lipids are absent from the acid-insoluble fraction because they are not polymers is wrong: they appear there as membrane vesicles.
Confusing doublets and triplets is a mistake: axoneme microtubules are doublets (9+2), while centriole fibrils are triplets (9+0).
Placing crossing over in zygotene is wrong: zygotene is synapsis, pachytene is crossing over, and chiasmata become visible in diplotene.
quick_revision: Cell theory: Schleiden + Schwann; Virchow added Omnis cellula-e cellula.
Prokaryotes: nucleoid, plasmids, mesosome, 70S ribosomes; no membrane-bound organelles.
Fluid mosaic model: Singer and Nicolson; quasi-fluid lipid bilayer with proteins.
Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles; SER makes lipids, RER makes proteins.
Golgi has cis (forming) and trans (maturing) faces; it forms glycoproteins and glycolipids.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes; cristae increase surface area.
Leucoplasts: amyloplast (starch), elaioplast (oil), aleuroplast (protein); chromoplast contains carotenoids.
Cilia and flagella are 9+2; centriole is 9+0 cartwheel with triplets.
Chromosomes by centromere: metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric.
Body element order: O > C > H > N; B-DNA has 10 bp per turn and 3.4 nm pitch.
Enzyme classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases; competitive inhibitor resembles substrate.
Cell cycle G1 → S → G2 → M; prophase I: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis.
